01.note: Bar Haddaya interpreted dreams favorably for those who paid him and unfavorably for those who did not. Abaye and Rava brought him the same dreams; Abaye paid and Rava did not, so Abaye heard of profit and honor, and Rava of loss, his wife's death and arrest, and the next day Rava was seized when the king's treasury was robbed. Alone, Rava was told he would take two blows, and blind men fighting struck him twice. Later he paid and heard good things. When bar Haddaya dropped a book saying all dreams follow the mouth, Rava called him a scoundrel, forgave all but his wife's death, and prayed he be handed to a merciless kingdom. Bar Haddaya fled to Rome, held back a reading from the king's unpaying wardrobe keeper, and was tied between two cedars and split in two.
01.why: The Gemara is collecting teachings on how dreams come true, such as which dreams are fulfilled and that dreams show a person's own thoughts. This story makes the point that a dream's outcome follows the way it is interpreted.

people.name: Bar Haddaya
people.about: An interpreter of dreams whose readings depended on whether he was paid.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Paid bar Haddaya and received favorable readings of his dreams.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Saw the same dreams as Abaye but did not pay at first, and received dire readings.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Father of Rava's wife, whose death bar Haddaya foretold.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; bar Haddaya asks for one as his fee.
Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn by men during prayer. One of the verses inside mentions a firstborn donkey.
Psalms of praise sung on festivals; the Egyptian hallel celebrates the Exodus from Egypt.
An academy of Torah study, led by a head who teaches the students.

02.note: A heretic told Rabbi Yishmael one dream after another, and each time Rabbi Yishmael read it as a confession: relations with his mother and his sister, kidnapping and selling an Israelite, adultery, and sending away two wives without a divorce. When Rabbi Yishmael said that peeling eggs meant he stripped the dead, the heretic said every reading was true except that one; just then a woman came and said the cloak he wore belonged to a man who had died and whom he had stripped. Last, he dreamed his father had left him property in Cappadocia. Learning that neither had ever been there, Rabbi Yishmael read the name as Greek for beam and ten, told him to look in the tenth beam, and he found it full of coins.
02.why: The Gemara has been gathering dream interpretations by Sages, including Rabbi Yishmael's reading of his nephew's dream. After these examples it turns to lists of what particular images in dreams signify.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: A Sage who interprets the heretic's dreams.

terms.meaning: Here, a man who rejected the Sages' teachings; the text does not name him.
A woman in the first stage of Jewish marriage, before she lives with her husband; relations with another man count as adultery.
A Jewish marriage ends only with a bill of divorce, called a get; sending a wife away without one leaves her still married.

03.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, each had a dream. Rav Pappa dreamed he entered a marsh and became head of a yeshiva; Rav Huna dreamed he entered a forest and became head of the advanced students. Some say both dreamed of a marsh, but Rav Pappa dreamed a drum hung from his neck and so became head of the yeshiva, while Rav Huna, who had no drum, led only the advanced students. Rav Ashi said that he had dreamed he entered a marsh, hung a drum and beat it.
03.why: The Gemara has just taught that dreaming of a marsh means one will head a yeshiva and dreaming of a forest means one will head the advanced students. These Sages' dreams are offered as cases where those signs came true.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Dreamed of a marsh and was appointed head of a yeshiva.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Dreamed of a forest and was appointed head of the advanced students.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Reports his own dream of entering a marsh and beating a drum.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study, led by a head who teaches the students.
The kalla: a gathering of the most accomplished students, taught by their own leader.

04.note: Rav Sheshet, who was blind, went along with everyone to greet the king. A heretic mocked him: whole jugs go to the river, but where do broken ones go? Rav Sheshet said he would show he knew more. Two troops passed with rising noise, and each time the heretic said the king was coming and Rav Sheshet said he was not. When a third passed in silence, Rav Sheshet said the king was surely coming now. Asked how he knew, he said earthly royalty is like heavenly royalty: God came to Elijah not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a still small voice. When the king came Rav Sheshet blessed him, and the heretic mocked him for blessing someone he could not see. Some say the heretic's friends gouged out his eyes; others, that Rav Sheshet fixed his gaze on him and he became a pile of bones.
04.why: The Gemara has just taught the blessing said on seeing a king and Rabbi Yoḥanan's advice to run to see even non-Jewish kings. Rav Sheshet goes and recites the blessing although he is blind.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: A blind Sage who goes to greet the king and outwits the heretic.

terms.meaning: Here, a man hostile to the Sages who mocks Rav Sheshet; the text does not name him.

05.note: Rabbi Sheila had a man flogged for having relations with a non-Jewish woman. The man told the king that a Jew was judging without royal authority, and Rabbi Sheila was summoned. He said the man had relations with a female donkey, and Elijah the prophet came, looking like a man, and testified. Told that such a man deserved death, Rabbi Sheila said Jews had no power to execute since their exile. While they deliberated he recited a verse and explained it as praise of God for granting earthly kingship; pleased, they gave him a staff and told him to judge. Leaving, the man asked if God does miracles for liars. Rabbi Sheila said gentiles are called donkeys, then saw the man was going to report this, declared him a pursuer, and struck him dead with the staff.
05.why: The Gemara has just told of Rav Sheshet, who said that royalty on earth is like royalty in heaven. Rabbi Sheila's praise of the king makes the same comparison, and afterward he expounds the verse that saved him.

people.name: Rabbi Sheila
people.about: A Sage who judged a Jewish man and was summoned by the king's officials.

people.name: Elijah the prophet
people.about: Appears as a man and testifies on Rabbi Sheila's behalf.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, someone trying to kill another; the Torah's rule is that one may kill him first. Rabbi Sheila says the man seeks to have him killed.
A name for God.
Given to Rabbi Sheila by the officials as a sign of his license to judge.

06.note: Ulla and Rav Ḥisda were walking past the doorway of the house of Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai, and Rav Ḥisda groaned and sighed. Ulla reminded him of teachings that sighing breaks half, or even all, of the body. Rav Ḥisda said he could not help it: this house once had sixty cooks by day and sixty by night for anyone in need, four doors open to every direction, and grain scattered outside in drought years so the embarrassed could take it at night, and its owner never took his hand from his pocket so a poor man of good family would not be shamed by waiting. Now it had fallen in ruins. Ulla quoted Rabbi Yoḥanan that the houses of the righteous were decreed to be destroyed with the Temple and will be restored; seeing him still unconsoled, he said: it is enough for a servant to be like his master.
06.why: The Gemara has just taught that one who sees Jewish houses in ruins recites the blessing 'the true Judge'. This story shows two Sages facing one such ruined house.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: Walks with Rav Ḥisda and tries to console him.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sighs at the sight of a ruined house he remembers as generous.

people.name: Rav Ḥana bar Ḥanilai
people.about: Owner of the house, famous for feeding the needy.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage whose teachings about sighing and ruined houses Ulla quotes.

terms.meaning: The Holy Temple in Jerusalem, God's house, which was destroyed; Ulla compares the ruined house to it.

07.note: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, met Rav Ḥanina, son of Rav Ika, on the road. They told him that on seeing him they had recited two blessings: the one for seeing a Sage, and 'Who has given us life'. He answered that he had regarded them as equal to six hundred thousand of Israel and recited three blessings, those two and 'Who knows all secrets'. They said: Are you all that clever? They fixed their gaze on him, and he died.
07.why: The Gemara has just taught that one who sees a friend after thirty days recites 'Who has given us life'. Here Sages use that blessing, with the blessing over Sages, on meeting a colleague.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Meets Rav Ḥanina on the road with Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Travels with Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Ḥanina, son of Rav Ika
people.about: The colleague they meet, who claims to have recited a third blessing over them.

terms.meaning: A blessing of thanks for reaching a special moment, said here on seeing a friend not seen for a while.
The blessing said on seeing a crowd of six hundred thousand Jews.

08.note: Rav Ketina was walking along the road when, at the entrance of a necromancer's house, an earthquake rumbled. He asked aloud whether the necromancer knew what this earthquake was. The necromancer called out: Ketina, Ketina, why would I not know? When God remembers His children suffering among the nations, He sheds two tears into the great sea, and the sound is heard from one end of the world to the other. That is an earthquake.
08.why: The mishna requires a blessing over zeva'ot, which Rav Ketina defines as earthquakes. Right after the story he calls the necromancer a liar, and the Gemara says he denied it only so people would not follow the necromancer.

people.name: Rav Ketina
people.about: A Sage who asks what an earthquake is and hears the necromancer's answer.

terms.meaning: Someone who claims to consult the dead.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses line by line.
A word in the mishna for a natural event over which one blesses God; Rav Ketina says it means an earthquake.

09.note: Hillel the Elder was coming along the road when he heard a scream in the city. He said: I am certain that it is not coming from my house. The Sages apply to him the verse 'He shall not be afraid of evil tidings; his heart is steadfast, trusting in the Lord', and Rava explains that the verse makes sense read from beginning to end or from end to beginning.
09.why: The mishna has just called it a vain prayer to ask, on hearing a scream, that it not be from one's own house. Hillel shows a different response: confidence instead of that prayer.

people.name: Hillel the Elder
people.about: A Sage who hears a scream and is sure it is not from his house.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who explains the verse applied to Hillel.

10.note: A student was walking behind Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, in the marketplace of Zion, and Rabbi Yishmael saw that he was afraid. He told him: You are a sinner, as it is written, 'The transgressors in Zion are afraid.' The student replied: Is it not written, 'Happy is the man that fears always'? Rabbi Yishmael answered that that verse is about matters of Torah.
10.why: The Gemara has just praised Hillel, whose trust in God left him unafraid of bad news. This story continues that theme and limits the verse praising constant fear to matters of Torah.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who rebukes a frightened student.

terms.meaning: Another name for Jerusalem.

11.note: Yehuda bar Natan was walking behind Rav Hamnuna and sighed. Rav Hamnuna said: Does this man want to bring suffering on himself? As it is written, 'For that which I did fear is come upon me.' Yehuda bar Natan answered: Is it not written, 'Happy is the man who fears always'? Rav Hamnuna replied that that verse is about matters of Torah.
11.why: This follows the story of the frightened student and Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei. It is a second case where a Sage rebukes a follower for fearing, and again the verse praising fear is limited to Torah.

people.name: Yehuda bar Natan
people.about: Walks behind Rav Hamnuna and sighs.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage who warns him that fear brings suffering.

12.note: Rabbi Abbahu went into a bathhouse, and its floor collapsed beneath him. A miracle happened: he stood on a pillar and saved one hundred and one men with one arm. He said: This is what Rav Aḥa meant.
12.why: Rav Aḥa has just taught that on leaving a bathhouse one thanks God for being saved from the fire. Rabbi Abbahu's rescue is offered as confirmation that such thanks are due.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage saved by a miracle when a bathhouse floor collapsed.

people.name: Rav Aḥa
people.about: A Sage whose teaching about thanks on leaving a bathhouse Rabbi Abbahu recalls.

terms.meaning: A public bath; the discussion treats entering one as a danger because of its fire.

13.note: Rabbi Akiva was traveling and came to a town where no one would give him lodging. He said: Everything God does is for the best, and slept in a field. He had a rooster, a donkey and a candle with him. The wind blew out the candle, a cat ate the rooster, and a lion ate the donkey, and he said again: Everything God does is for the best. That night an army came and took the town captive. He said to them: Didn't I tell you? Everything God does is for the best. The translation explains that he was spared because no light or animal gave away where he was.
13.why: The Gemara is bringing verses showing that one blesses God for bad things as well as good. Rav Huna, quoting Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Akiva, teaches that one should always say 'everything God does is for the best', and this incident is its example.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who keeps saying everything God does is for the best through a night of losses.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reports the teaching that one should always say this.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the mishna, the main early collection of Jewish law.

14.note: When Rome decreed that Jews may not study Torah, Pappos ben Yehuda found Rabbi Akiva teaching it to public gatherings and asked if he feared the empire. Rabbi Akiva told a parable: a fox invited fish fleeing nets onto dry land, and they answered that if they feared in the water where they live, all the more where they would die; Torah is Israel's life. Soon both were jailed, and Pappos said Rabbi Akiva was fortunate to be held for Torah, while he was held for idle matters. As Rabbi Akiva was executed, his flesh raked with iron combs, he recited the Shema, telling his students he had long waited to fulfill 'with all your soul'. He died on the word 'One', and a heavenly voice praised him. The angels protested, God answered them, and a voice said he was destined for the World-to-Come.
14.why: The mishna and a baraita have just read 'with all your soul' as Rabbi Akiva did: love God even if He takes your soul. This story shows Rabbi Akiva living out that reading at his death.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage who keeps teaching Torah under Roman decree and is executed.

people.name: Pappos ben Yehuda
people.about: Warns Rabbi Akiva about the empire and is later jailed with him.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who answers the angels' protest.

terms.meaning: The central Jewish declaration of faith, said daily: 'Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One.'
A voice from heaven that announces God's judgment.
The angels who serve before God.
The life after this world in which the righteous are rewarded.

15.note: In Rabba's bathroom the bricks were laid east and west, so that he would face north and south. Abaye moved them to north and south; Rabba came in, put them back and asked who was upsetting him, saying he followed Rabbi Akiva, who forbade facing east and west anywhere. In a separate account, Rabbi Akiva recalled following his teacher Rabbi Yehoshua into the bathroom and learning three things from watching him: face north or south, uncover yourself only when sitting, and wipe with the left hand. Ben Azzai asked whether he had been so bold with his teacher, and Rabbi Akiva answered: It is Torah, and I must learn.
15.why: The Gemara has just set out a dispute over which directions one may face when relieving oneself, with Rabbi Akiva forbidding east and west even outside the Land of Israel. Rabba follows his ruling, and Rabbi Akiva's own account shows where he learned it.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: A Sage who insisted on the direction of his bathroom bricks.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Moves Rabba's bricks.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Learned bathroom practice by following his teacher.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's teacher.

people.name: Ben Azzai
people.about: Challenges Rabbi Akiva for watching his teacher so closely.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages not included in the mishna, the main early collection of Jewish law.

15.flag: Joins two separate incidents with different people: Rabba and Abaye's bricks, and Rabbi Akiva following Rabbi Yehoshua.

16.note: Rav Kahana went in and lay under Rav's bed. He heard Rav chatting and laughing with his wife and having relations with her. Rav Kahana said that Rav acted like one who had never eaten a cooked dish. Rav said: Kahana, you are here? Leave, this is not proper behavior. Rav Kahana answered: It is Torah, and I must learn.
16.why: The Gemara has just told of Rabbi Akiva and Ben Azzai following their teachers into the bathroom and defending it with 'It is Torah, and I must learn'. Rav Kahana uses the same words for an even more private intrusion.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Hides under Rav's bed to learn how he behaves.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage he watches, who tells him to leave.

terms.meaning: Rav's own name, which Rav Kahana uses here.

17.note: There was a bathroom in Tiberias where, when two people went in together, they were harmed, even by day. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi each went in alone and were not harmed. The Sages asked them: Aren't you afraid? They said they had a tradition: for the bathroom, modesty and silence; for suffering, silence and prayer.
17.why: Rabbi Tanḥum bar Ḥanilai has just said that one who is modest in the bathroom is saved from snakes, scorpions and demons. These two Sages, safe in a dangerous bathroom, show that protection at work.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Entered the dangerous bathroom alone and was not harmed.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Entered the dangerous bathroom alone and was not harmed.

18.note: Before Rava became head of the yeshiva, his wife, the daughter of Rav Ḥisda, would rattle a nut in a copper vessel for him when he went to the bathroom. After he became head, she made a window for him and placed her hand on his head.
18.why: The Gemara is telling how people guarded against demons in the bathroom, as Abaye's mother did by raising a lamb to go with him. This is another such precaution, made greater once Rava held higher office.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage whose wife protected him in the bathroom.

people.name: The daughter of Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rava's wife, who devised the protections.

terms.meaning: An academy of Torah study, led by a head who teaches the students.

19.note: A eulogizer came to speak before Rav Naḥman and said of the dead man that he was modest in his ways. Rav Naḥman said to him: Did you go into the bathroom with him, that you know whether he was modest or not? He cited a teaching that only one who is modest in the bathroom may be called modest.
19.why: The Gemara is discussing modesty when relieving oneself. Right afterward it explains Rav Naḥman's insistence: eulogizers are punished along with the dead for praising virtues the dead did not have.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: A Sage who challenges a eulogizer's praise of the dead.

terms.meaning: A person who speaks in praise of the dead at a funeral.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the mishna, the main early collection of Jewish law.

20.note: Rav Safra was in a bathroom when Rabbi Abba came along and coughed by the door. Rav Safra said: Enter, master. When he came out, Rabbi Abba rebuked him: You have never gone to Seir, yet you have learned the ways of Seir? He cited the teaching about the Temple's bathroom of honor, where a locked door meant someone was inside and an open one meant no one was, which shows that speaking in the bathroom is not proper.
20.why: The Gemara is gathering rules of modesty in the bathroom. Right afterward it defends Rav Safra: he spoke because making Rabbi Abba wait could endanger his health.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Was in the bathroom and invited Rabbi Abba in.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Rebukes Rav Safra for speaking in the bathroom.

terms.meaning: The land of the Edomites, who the translation says were not strict about modesty.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses line by line.
The Holy Temple in Jerusalem.
